# Kaṇaverajātaka (Ja 318)

**ID:** Ja 318
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Kaṇaverajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Flowering Oleander
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja318
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kaṇaverajātaka* (Ja 318) is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection told by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana concerning a monk tempted by thoughts of his former wife, with the introductory narrative noting that the background circumstances are detailed in the *Indriyajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The central tale recounts an unusual past life in which the Bodhisatta was born under the astrological sign of a thief and became a desperate, notorious highway robber in Kāsi [Narada 2008; Appleton 2010; Sujato 2011]. Captured and condemned to death, he was led to execution wearing a wreath of red oleander (*kaṇavera*) blossoms, which gave the story its name [Cowell 1897; Sujato 2011]. A wealthy courtesan named Sāmā fell passionately in love with him, successfully bribed the authorities to spare him, and lived with him [Kariyawasam 2003; Appleton 2010; Sujato 2011]. Suspicious that her unfaithfulness might lead her to betray him as she had others, the robber later lured her into a thicket of *kaṇavera* bushes, choked her unconscious, stole her jewelry, and escaped; despite her attempts to woo him back, he refused to return [Appleton 2010; Cowell 1897]. Buddhist commentators and modern scholars frequently cite the narrative as a rare depiction of the Bodhisatta committing serious wrongdoing, reflecting the doctrinal idea that unenlightened Bodhisattas retain mortal flaws due to astrological or karmic circumstances [Narada 2008; Appleton 2010; Chen 2015].

In terms of parallels and textual relations, SuttaCentral identifies a full parallel in the Sanskrit Mahāvastu (Mvu 50, the *Śyāmā Jātaka*) [SuttaCentral], a connection also analyzed by J. J. Jones [Jones 1952]. A comparison with a passage in the *Mahābhārata* describing a courtesan abandoned by her lover was suggested by J. Mehlig, though the names and plots diverge [Söhnen-Thieme]. The narrative motifs are also referenced in related Pali narratives, such as the *Sulasājātaka* (Ja 419) [Cowell 1897; Sujato 2011]. DharmaNexus records Pali-internal text reuse with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (eight matches totaling 718 characters), while showing no machine matches meeting the score threshold in non-Pali corpora [DharmaNexus].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels (SuttaCentral): San Lo Mvu 50 Śyāmā Jātaka
- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Tatiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a3) (§2.1–2.6 ↔ §466–468)

**Sources**

- [Narada 2008] Narada Mahathera, The Buddha and His Teachings (Revised 2008) — Discusses Bodhisatta depicted as a desperate robber in Ja 318.
- [Kariyawasam 2003] Tilokasundari Kariyawasam, Buddhism and Psychology (2003) — Summary of Sāmā falling in love with the condemned thief.
- [Chen 2015] Lang Chen, Heroic Sinners: Evil in Buddhist Narrative Literature (2015) — Notes the Bodhisatta's robber birth being attributed to his horoscope.
- [Appleton 2010] Naomi Appleton, Jātaka Stories in Theravada Buddhism: Narrating the Bodhisatta Path (2010) — Summary of plot (robber knocked courtesan unconscious and stole jewels; moral on betrayal).
- [Cowell 1897] E. B. Cowell (ed.), The Jātaka, or Stories of the Buddha's Former Births, Vol. 3 (1897) — Details of the kanavera flowers, execution, theft, and cross-reference in Sulasa Jātaka.
